title: Differentiation I: limits and the rules

problems.html:
Evaluate, cancelling a common factor or rationalising first where needed:

  1. lim⁡x→2x2−4x−2\displaystyle\lim_{x\to2}\frac{x^2-4}{x-2}x→2lim​x−2x2−4​;

  2. lim⁡x→3x2−9x2−x−6\displaystyle\lim_{x\to3}\frac{x^2-9}{x^2-x-6}x→3lim​x2−x−6x2−9​;

  3. lim⁡x→0x+1−1x\displaystyle\lim_{x\to0}\frac{\sqrt{x+1}-1}{x}x→0lim​xx+1​−1​;

  4. lim⁡x→0sin⁡5xx\displaystyle\lim_{x\to0}\frac{\sin 5x}{x}x→0lim​xsin5x​.
hints: Substituting directly gives 00\tfrac0000​ in each of the first three, which is a signal to rewrite rather than a verdict that the limit fails.
In (a) and (b), factorise top and bottom and cancel the common factor — legitimate because xxx approaches the point without ever reaching it.

In (c) multiply top and bottom by x+1+1\sqrt{x+1}+1x+1​+1 to clear the root; in (d) force the standard limit into view by writing sin⁡5xx=5⋅sin⁡5x5x\dfrac{\sin 5x}{x}=5\cdot\dfrac{\sin 5x}{5x}xsin5x​=5⋅5xsin5x​.
problems.format: (a)–(d), comma-separated; fractions

problems.html:
1. Find lim⁡x→0+1x\displaystyle\lim_{x\to0^{+}}\frac1xx→0+lim​x1​ and lim⁡x→0−1x\displaystyle\lim_{x\to0^{-}}\frac1xx→0−lim​x1​, and state the vertical asymptote.

  2. For f(x)={x2,x<12x,x≥1f(x)=\begin{cases}x^2,&x<1\\ 2x,&x\ge1\end{cases}f(x)={x2,2x,​x<1x≥1​ find the one-sided limits at x=1x=1x=1 and decide whether lim⁡x→1f(x)\lim_{x\to1}f(x)limx→1​f(x) exists.

  3. Divide by the highest power of xxx in the denominator to find lim⁡x→∞2x+1x2+3\displaystyle\lim_{x\to\infty}\frac{2x+1}{x^2+3}x→∞lim​x2+32x+1​ and lim⁡x→∞4x3−x2x3+7\displaystyle\lim_{x\to\infty}\frac{4x^3-x}{2x^3+7}x→∞lim​2x3+74x3−x​, and state each horizontal asymptote y=Ly=Ly=L.
hints: A one-sided limit asks what happens as xxx approaches from one side only, so the two sides can disagree.
For (b), evaluate each formula at the joining point: use x2x^2x2 from the left and 2x2x2x from the right. The two-sided limit exists only if the two agree.
For (c), divide every term, top and bottom, by the highest power of xxx in the denominator; each term of the form 1/xk1/x^k1/xk then vanishes as x→∞x\to\inftyx→∞.
problems.format: (b) left, right limits, then (c) both limits

problems.html:
Find the constant that makes each function continuous everywhere.

  1. f(x)=x2−1x−1f(x)=\dfrac{x^2-1}{x-1}f(x)=x−1x2−1​ for x≠1x\ne1x=1, and f(1)=kf(1)=kf(1)=k.

  2. g(x)={cx+1,x≤2x2,x>2.g(x)=\begin{cases}cx+1,&x\le2\\ x^2,&x>2.\end{cases}g(x)={cx+1,x2,​x≤2x>2.​
hints: Continuity at a point means the limit there exists and equals the value assigned to the function.
In (a) simplify the fraction for x≠1x\neq1x=1 first; the limit is then obvious, and kkk must be set equal to it.
In (b) the two pieces must agree where they meet, so evaluate both formulas at x=2x=2x=2 and set them equal.
problems.format: k, then c — comma-separated

problems.html: Using f′(x)=lim⁡δx→0f(x+δx)−f(x)δxf'(x)=\lim_{\delta x\to0}\dfrac{f(x+\delta x)-f(x)}{\delta x}f′(x)=limδx→0​δxf(x+δx)−f(x)​, differentiate from first principles: (a) f(x)=x2−3xf(x)=x^2-3xf(x)=x2−3x;(b) f(x)=1xf(x)=\dfrac1xf(x)=x1​.
hints: Write out the difference quotient in full before simplifying anything — that is where the method lives.
In (a) expand (x+δx)2(x+\delta x)^2(x+δx)2 and watch the x2x^2x2 terms cancel, leaving every surviving term with a factor of δx\delta xδx.
In (b) combine the two fractions over the common denominator x(x+δx)x(x+\delta x)x(x+δx) first; the numerator collapses to −δx-\delta x−δx, which then cancels.
problems.format: f′(2) for (a), then for (b)

problems.html: Write down the derivative of each (use a power where helpful): (a) x5,(b) x,(c) 1x3,(d) e2x,(e) ln⁡x,(f) sin⁡3x,(g) cos⁡x2,(h) tan⁡x,(i) cosh⁡x.\begin{gather*} \text{(a) } x^5,\quad \text{(b) } \sqrt{x},\quad \text{(c) } \frac{1}{x^3},\quad \text{(d) } \mathrm{e}^{2x},\quad \text{(e) } \ln x,\\ \text{(f) } \sin 3x,\quad \text{(g) } \cos\tfrac{x}{2},\quad \text{(h) } \tan x,\quad \text{(i) } \cosh x. \end{gather*}(a) x5,(b) x​,(c) x31​,(d) e2x,(e) lnx,(f) sin3x,(g) cos2x​,(h) tanx,(i) coshx.​ (j) For y=x4y=x^4y=x4, list y′, y′′, y′′′, y(4), y(5)y',\,y'',\,y''',\,y^{(4)},\,y^{(5)}y′,y′′,y′′′,y(4),y(5).
hints: Rewrite roots and reciprocals as powers first: x=x1/2\sqrt x=x^{1/2}x​=x1/2 and 1/x3=x−31/x^3=x^{-3}1/x3=x−3, so the power rule applies to both.
Wherever the argument is not simply xxx, a chain-rule factor appears: differentiating sin⁡3x\sin 3xsin3x brings out a 333, and cos⁡x2\cos\tfrac{x}{2}cos2x​ brings out a 12\tfrac1221​.

The last three are standard results: tan⁡\tantan gives sec⁡2\sec^2sec2, and cosh⁡\coshcosh gives sinh⁡\sinhsinh with no minus sign. In (j) each differentiation lowers the power by one, and a polynomial eventually differentiates to 000.
problems.format: (d),(f),(g) at x = 0, then y‴(1) in (j)

problems.html: Name uuu and vvv each time. Product rule (uv)′=u′v+uv′(uv)'=u'v+uv'(uv)′=u′v+uv′: (a) x2exx^2\mathrm{e}^{x}x2ex;(b) xsin⁡xx\sin xxsinx. Quotient rule (uv)′=u′v−uv′v2\left(\tfrac{u}{v}\right)'=\dfrac{u'v-uv'}{v^2}(vu​)′=v2u′v−uv′​: (c) xx+1\dfrac{x}{x+1}x+1x​; (d) sin⁡xx\dfrac{\sin x}{x}xsinx​.
hints: The product rule is (uv)′=u′v+uv′(uv)'=u'v+uv'(uv)′=u′v+uv′ — two terms, not u′v′u'v'u′v′. The quotient rule is u′v−uv′v2\dfrac{u'v-uv'}{v^2}v2u′v−uv′​, where the minus sign makes the order matter.
Name uuu and vvv explicitly and write down u′u'u′ and v′v'v′ before assembling anything; most errors come from losing track of which factor has been differentiated.
In (a) both terms share a factor of xexx\mathrm{e}^{x}xex; in (c) the numerator 1⋅(x+1)−x⋅11\cdot(x+1)-x\cdot11⋅(x+1)−x⋅1 collapses to a constant.
problems.format: each at x = 1: 3 d.p., but (c) as a fraction

problems.html: Differentiate: (a) (3x+1)5(3x+1)^5(3x+1)5;(b) ex2\mathrm{e}^{x^2}ex2;(c) sin⁡(x2)\sin(x^2)sin(x2); (d) ln⁡(1+x2)\ln(1+x^2)ln(1+x2).
hints: The chain rule says: differentiate the outer function, leaving the inner one alone, then multiply by the derivative of the inner.
Identify the inner function first each time — 3x+13x+13x+1, then x2x^2x2, then x2x^2x2 again, then 1+x21+x^21+x2.
The inner derivative is the factor most often dropped: in (a) it supplies the 333, and in (b), (c) and (d) it supplies the 2x2x2x.
problems.format: (a) and (d) at x = 1

problems.html: Find  dy dx\frac{\,\mathrm{d}y}{\,\mathrm{d}x}dxdy​: (a) parametrically, for x=cos⁡t, y=sin⁡tx=\cos t,\ y=\sin tx=cost, y=sint; (b) implicitly, for xy=1xy=1xy=1; (c) logarithmically, for y=xxy=x^{x}y=xx, x>0x>0x>0.
hints: Three techniques, each with its own trigger. Parametric: divide the two ttt-derivatives. Implicit: differentiate both sides with respect to xxx, treating yyy as a function of xxx. Logarithmic: take logs first.
In (b), xyxyxy is a product, so the product rule applies — and differentiating yyy produces a factor dydx\dfrac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x}dxdy​ by the chain rule.
In (c) the exponent is not constant, so the power rule fails. Since x>0x>0x>0, take ln⁡\lnln of both sides, differentiate, then multiply back by yyy.

problems.html:
Both parts turn on the one-sided limits of the difference quotient at the join.

  1. Let f(x)={x2,x≤1ax+b,x>1.f(x)=\begin{cases}x^2,&x\le1\\ ax+b,&x>1.\end{cases}f(x)={x2,ax+b,​x≤1x>1.​ Find a,ba,ba,b so that fff is differentiable at x=1x=1x=1. Why is your fff automatically continuous there?

  2. Using the one-sided limits of the difference quotient at 000, show that ReLU⁡(x)=max⁡(0,x)\operatorname{ReLU}(x)=\max(0,x)ReLU(x)=max(0,x) is continuous at 000 but not differentiable there.
hints: A function differentiable at a point is continuous there, so in (a) first make the two pieces meet at x=1x=1x=1: that gives one equation in aaa and bbb.

Then form the difference quotient f(1+δx)−f(1)δx\dfrac{f(1+\delta x)-f(1)}{\delta x}δxf(1+δx)−f(1)​ separately for δx<0\delta x<0δx<0 (use x2x^2x2) and for δx>0\delta x>0δx>0 (use ax+bax+bax+b), and let δx→0\delta x\to0δx→0 from each side.
For (b), write ReLU⁡(δx)\operatorname{ReLU}(\delta x)ReLU(δx) out separately for δx<0\delta x<0δx<0 and δx>0\delta x>0δx>0, and simplify the difference quotient on each side before taking the limit.
problems.format: a, b, then (b)'s left and right limits

problems.html:
Let f(x)=xf(x)=\sqrt{x}f(x)=x​.

  1. Show from first principles that f′(x)=12xf'(x)=\dfrac{1}{2\sqrt x}f′(x)=2x​1​.

  2. Hence find the equation of the tangent line to y=xy=\sqrt{x}y=x​ at x=4x=4x=4.
hints: For (a), the difference quotient contains a difference of square roots — multiply top and bottom by the conjugate to clear it.
The numerator then becomes just δx\delta xδx, which cancels, and letting δx→0\delta x\to0δx→0 makes the two roots coincide.
For (b) you need a point and a slope: evaluate fff and f′f'f′ at x=4x=4x=4, then use y−y0=m(x−x0)y-y_0=m(x-x_0)y−y0​=m(x−x0​).
problems.format: the tangent's slope, then its y-intercept

problems.html:
A particle moves along a line with displacement s(t)=t3−6t2+9ts(t)=t^3-6t^2+9ts(t)=t3−6t2+9t metres, t≥0t\ge0t≥0 seconds.

  1. Find the velocity v(t)=s˙v(t)=\dot sv(t)=s˙ and acceleration a(t)=s¨a(t)=\ddot sa(t)=s¨.

  2. When is the particle momentarily at rest?

  3. In which direction is it moving at t=2t=2t=2?

  4. Give the acceleration at each rest instant and interpret its sign.
hints: Velocity is the derivative of displacement and acceleration the derivative of velocity, so differentiate twice.
Momentarily at rest means v=0v=0v=0, so factorise the quadratic rather than reaching for the formula.
The sign of vvv gives the direction of travel, while the sign of aaa at each rest instant says whether the particle is about to turn back or is being pushed forwards again.
problems.format: the two rest times; then v(2)

problems.html:
1. The logistic function is σ(x)=11+e−x\sigma(x)=\dfrac{1}{1+\mathrm{e}^{-x}}σ(x)=1+e−x1​. Show, using the chain rule, that σ′(x)=σ(x)(1−σ(x))\sigma'(x)=\sigma(x)\bigl(1-\sigma(x)\bigr)σ′(x)=σ(x)(1−σ(x)).

  2. A model’s error is L(w)=(w−3)2+1L(w)=(w-3)^2+1L(w)=(w−3)2+1. Compute  dL dw\frac{\,\mathrm{d}L}{\,\mathrm{d}w}dwdL​ and evaluate it at w=5w=5w=5. Reading the derivative as a sensitivity, should a small gradient-descent step increase or decrease www? Write out the gradient-descent update w←w−η  dL dww\leftarrow w-\eta\,\frac{\,\mathrm{d}L}{\,\mathrm{d}w}w←w−ηdwdL​ (learning rate η>0\eta>0η>0) for this LLL. (Unit 8 develops the method, including how large η\etaη may be.)

  3. During training a loss decays as ℓ(t)=e−t/5\ell(t)=\mathrm{e}^{-t/5}ℓ(t)=e−t/5, where ttt is the epoch number. Find the rate of change ℓ′(t)\ell'(t)ℓ′(t), evaluate it at t=0t=0t=0 and t=5t=5t=5, and say what the two values tell you about training.
hints: For (a) write σ=(1+e−x)−1\sigma=(1+\mathrm{e}^{-x})^{-1}σ=(1+e−x)−1 and apply the chain rule, remembering that the derivative of e−x\mathrm{e}^{-x}e−x carries a minus sign; then compare with 1−σ=e−x1+e−x1-\sigma=\dfrac{\mathrm{e}^{-x}}{1+\mathrm{e}^{-x}}1−σ=1+e−xe−x​.
For (b) differentiate the quadratic and evaluate it. A positive derivative means the error grows with www nearby, so a small step must go the other way — which is why gradient descent subtracts.
For (c) the exponent is −t/5-t/5−t/5, so the chain rule contributes a factor −15-\tfrac15−51​. Both rates come out negative, since the loss is falling; compare their sizes.
problems.format: dL/dw at 5, ℓ′(0), then ℓ′(5) to 3 d.p.

problems.html:
Each line contains one mistake. Identify it and give the correct derivative.

  1. “ d dx(x2+1)3=3(x2+1)2\frac{\,\mathrm{d}}{\,\mathrm{d}x}(x^2+1)^3=3(x^2+1)^2dxd​(x2+1)3=3(x2+1)2.”

  2. “ d dx(x2ex)=2x ex\frac{\,\mathrm{d}}{\,\mathrm{d}x}\bigl(x^2\mathrm{e}^{x}\bigr)=2x\,\mathrm{e}^{x}dxd​(x2ex)=2xex.”

  3. “ d dx(sin⁡xcos⁡x)=cos⁡x (−sin⁡x)\frac{\,\mathrm{d}}{\,\mathrm{d}x}\bigl(\sin x\cos x\bigr)=\cos x\,(-\sin x)dxd​(sinxcosx)=cosx(−sinx).”
hints: Each line has forgotten one rule. Name the structure of the expression first — a composition, a product, a product — and the missing rule names itself.
In (a) the outer power was differentiated but the inner function was not; in (b) only the first half of the product rule was written down.
In (c) the two derivatives were multiplied together instead of the product rule being applied. The correct answer simplifies to a familiar double-angle expression.
problems.format: the correct (a) and (c) at x = 1, to 3 d.p.

problems.html: Differentiate y=(2x−1)4x2+1\displaystyle y=\frac{(2x-1)^4}{x^2+1}y=x2+1(2x−1)4​, simplifying as far as possible.
hints: This needs both rules: the quotient rule on the whole, and the chain rule inside it to differentiate (2x−1)4(2x-1)^4(2x−1)4.
Differentiating (2x−1)4(2x-1)^4(2x−1)4 gives 4(2x−1)3⋅24(2x-1)^3\cdot24(2x−1)3⋅2 — the factor of 222 from the inner function is the one most often dropped.
Before expanding anything, take the common factor (2x−1)3(2x-1)^3(2x−1)3 out of the numerator; what is left in the bracket is only a quadratic.
problems.format: the derivative at x = 1

problems.html:
The folium of Descartes is x3+y3=6xyx^3+y^3=6xyx3+y3=6xy.

  1. Find  dy dx\frac{\,\mathrm{d}y}{\,\mathrm{d}x}dxdy​ by implicit differentiation.

  2. Hence find the slope of the curve at the point (3,3)(3,3)(3,3).
hints: Differentiate every term with respect to xxx, treating yyy as a function of xxx throughout.
So y3y^3y3 needs the chain rule, giving 3y2y′3y^2y'3y2y′, and the right-hand side 6xy6xy6xy needs the product rule, giving 6y+6xy′6y+6xy'6y+6xy′.
Now gather every term containing y′y'y′ on one side, factor y′y'y′ out, and divide — then substitute the point.
problems.format: the slope of the curve at (3,3)

problems.html:
A curve is given by x=t2, y=t3−3tx=t^2,\ y=t^3-3tx=t2, y=t3−3t.

  1. Find  dy dx\frac{\,\mathrm{d}y}{\,\mathrm{d}x}dxdy​ in terms of ttt.

  2. Find the point(s) with a horizontal tangent and the point(s) with a vertical tangent.
hints: For a parametric curve, dydx=dy/dtdx/dt\dfrac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x}=\dfrac{\mathrm{d}y/\mathrm{d}t}{\mathrm{d}x/\mathrm{d}t}dxdy​=dx/dtdy/dt​ — differentiate each coordinate with respect to ttt and divide.

A horizontal tangent needs dy/dt=0\mathrm{d}y/\mathrm{d}t=0dy/dt=0 with dx/dt≠0\mathrm{d}x/\mathrm{d}t\neq0dx/dt=0; a vertical one needs the reverse. Checking the other derivative is not optional, since both vanishing at once means something else entirely.
Solve dy/dt=0\mathrm{d}y/\mathrm{d}t=0dy/dt=0 and dx/dt=0\mathrm{d}x/\mathrm{d}t=0dx/dt=0 separately, then substitute each ttt back into the original equations to get the actual points.
problems.format: the two horizontal points; then the vertical one

problems.html: Use logarithmic differentiation to differentiate y=(x2+1)3(2x−1)4 e−5x\displaystyle y=(x^2+1)^3(2x-1)^4\,\mathrm{e}^{-5x}y=(x2+1)3(2x−1)4e−5x.
hints: Taking logarithms turns the product of three factors into a sum of three terms, which is far easier to differentiate.
So write ln⁡∣y∣=3ln⁡(x2+1)+4ln⁡∣2x−1∣−5x\ln|y|=3\ln(x^2+1)+4\ln|2x-1|-5xln∣y∣=3ln(x2+1)+4ln∣2x−1∣−5x and differentiate both sides.
The left-hand side gives y′y\dfrac{y'}{y}yy′​ by the chain rule, so multiply back through by yyy — and remember yyy is the original expression.
problems.format: the derivative at x = 1, to 3 d.p.

problems.html: For each function, find every point where the graph breaks (the function is undefined there, or is defined but not continuous) and classify the break as removable (the two one-sided limits exist and agree, but the function is undefined there or takes a different value), a jump (both one-sided limits exist but differ), or infinite (a one-sided limit is ±∞\pm\infty±∞, so the graph has a vertical asymptote). (a) f(x)=x−2x2−4,(b) g(x)=1x−1,(c) h(x)={x,x<0x+2,x≥0.\text{(a) }f(x)=\frac{x-2}{x^2-4},\qquad\allowbreak \text{(b) }g(x)=\frac{1}{x-1},\qquad\allowbreak \text{(c) }h(x)=\begin{cases}x,&x<0\\ x+2,&x\ge0.\end{cases}(a) f(x)=x2−4x−2​,(b) g(x)=x−11​,(c) h(x)={x,x+2,​x<0x≥0.​
hints: Start with the points where the function is undefined — but a function defined everywhere can still break, so check any point where its rule changes as well.

Then decide the type: if the two-sided limit exists but the value is missing or wrong, the break is removable; if the two one-sided limits are finite but different, it is a jump; if either runs off to infinity, it is infinite.
In (a) cancel the common factor first — that reveals two different points behaving in two different ways.
problems.format: (a) at 2, (a) at −2, then (b), then (c)

problems.html:
State whether each is true or false, with a one-line reason.

  1. If fff is continuous at aaa then fff is differentiable at aaa.

  2. (uv)′=u′v′(uv)'=u'v'(uv)′=u′v′.

  3. For lim⁡x→af(x)\lim_{x\to a}f(x)limx→a​f(x) to exist, f(a)f(a)f(a) must be defined.

  4. If lim⁡x→∞f(x)=L\lim_{x\to\infty}f(x)=Llimx→∞​f(x)=L then y=Ly=Ly=L is a horizontal asymptote.

  5.  d dxxn=nxn−1\frac{\,\mathrm{d}}{\,\mathrm{d}x}x^{n}=nx^{n-1}dxd​xn=nxn−1 holds only for integer nnn.

  6. f(x)=x1/3f(x)=x^{1/3}f(x)=x1/3 is differentiable at x=0x=0x=0.
hints: Five of the six are false, and each falls to a single well-chosen example — think of ∣x∣|x|∣x∣, and of x1/3x^{1/3}x1/3.
For (i), continuity does not force a tangent to exist: a corner is continuous but has no single slope. The implication runs the other way.
For (v), the power rule holds for every real exponent, not just whole numbers; and for (vi), ask what happens to the slope of x1/3x^{1/3}x1/3 as xxx approaches zero.
problems.format: (i)–(vi): true or false, comma-separated

problems.html: Differentiate (state the rule used): (a) ex2sin⁡x,(b) x2ln⁡x,(c) xx2+1,(d) e−xcos⁡2x,(e) ln⁡xx,(f) 1+x (x>0).\text{(a) }\mathrm{e}^{x^2}\sin x,\quad\allowbreak \text{(b) }x^2\ln x,\quad\allowbreak \text{(c) }\frac{x}{\sqrt{x^2+1}},\quad\allowbreak \text{(d) }\mathrm{e}^{-x}\cos 2x,\quad\allowbreak \text{(e) }\frac{\ln x}{x},\quad\allowbreak \text{(f) }\sqrt{1+\sqrt{x}}\ (x>0).(a) ex2sinx,(b) x2lnx,(c) x2+1​x​,(d) e−xcos2x,(e) xlnx​,(f) 1+x​​ (x>0).
hints: Identify the structure of each before differentiating: which are products, which quotients, which compositions — and which need two rules together.

(a) and (d) are products with a chain rule inside a factor; (c) and (e) are quotients, and in (c) the denominator v=(x2+1)1/2v=(x^2+1)^{1/2}v=(x2+1)1/2 itself needs the chain rule; (f) is a composition with a composition inside it.

In (c), multiply top and bottom by x2+1\sqrt{x^2+1}x2+1​ to clear the inner fraction. In (f) work from the outside in: differentiate u\sqrt{u}u​, then multiply by the derivative of u=1+xu=1+\sqrt xu=1+x​.
problems.format: (c), (f) at x = 1 to 3 d.p., then (d) at x = 0

problems.html:
1. For x=2t, y=t2−1x=2t,\ y=t^2-1x=2t, y=t2−1 find  dy dx\frac{\,\mathrm{d}y}{\,\mathrm{d}x}dxdy​ and  d2y dx2\frac{\,\mathrm{d}^{2} y}{\,\mathrm{d}x^{2}}dx2d2y​.

hints: The first derivative is dydx=dy/dtdx/dt\dfrac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x}=\dfrac{\mathrm{d}y/\mathrm{d}t}{\mathrm{d}x/\mathrm{d}t}dxdy​=dx/dtdy/dt​, both taken with respect to the parameter.

In (b) you will need ddt(−cot⁡t)=csc⁡2t\dfrac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}(-\cot t)=\csc^2 tdtd​(−cott)=csc2t before dividing by dx/dt=−rsin⁡t\mathrm{d}x/\mathrm{d}t=-r\sin tdx/dt=−rsint.

questions.stem: lim⁡x→3x2−9x−3=6\displaystyle\lim_{x\to3}\frac{x^2-9}{x-3}=6x→3lim​x−3x2−9​=6, and yet the function is undefined at x=3x=3x=3. Is that a contradiction?
options: Yes — a limit cannot exist where the function has no value.
No: a limit describes what fff approaches near the point, and ignores f(3)f(3)f(3) entirely.
No, but only because this particular discontinuity happens to be removable.
Yes, unless the function is first redefined at x=3x=3x=3.
questions.hint: Look at the definition of a limit and ask whether the value f(3)f(3)f(3) appears in it anywhere.
questions.why: The definition of a limit looks only at xxx near aaa, never at aaa itself — which is exactly what makes cancelling the common factor legitimate. Here x2−9x−3=x+3\dfrac{x^2-9}{x-3}=x+3x−3x2−9​=x+3 at every x≠3x\neq3x=3, so the values approach 666 even though nothing is assigned at 333. The break is indeed removable, and one could define f(3)=6f(3)=6f(3)=6 to make the function continuous; but that is a separate act of repair, and the limit existed perfectly well before it.

questions.stem: fff is continuous at aaa. Does it follow that fff is differentiable at aaa?
options: Yes — continuity and differentiability are two names for the same condition.
No, and the implication fails in the other direction too.
No: ∣x∣|x|∣x∣ is continuous at 000 but has a corner there, so no single tangent exists.
Yes, provided fff is defined on both sides of aaa.
questions.hint: Try to draw a tangent to y=∣x∣y=|x|y=∣x∣ at the origin — then ask whether the graph is broken there.
questions.why: At 000 the function ∣x∣|x|∣x∣ has left slope −1-1−1 and right slope +1+1+1; the two disagree, so there is no derivative, even though the graph is unbroken. Differentiability is therefore strictly the stronger condition. The converse direction does hold — a differentiable function is automatically continuous — which is why the last option is wrong. The same corner appears in ReLU⁡\operatorname{ReLU}ReLU, differentiable everywhere except at 000, where in practice the value is simply fixed by convention.

questions.stem: A student differentiates x2exx^2\mathrm{e}^{x}x2ex and writes 2x ex2x\,\mathrm{e}^{x}2xex. What has gone wrong?
options: The chain rule should have been used instead of the product rule.
Only the first half of the product rule was kept; the term x2exx^2\mathrm{e}^{x}x2ex is missing.
Nothing — that answer is correct.
The derivative of ex\mathrm{e}^{x}ex is not ex\mathrm{e}^{x}ex.
questions.hint: The product rule (uv)′=u′v+uv′(uv)'=u'v+uv'(uv)′=u′v+uv′ has two terms. Write both of them out with u=x2u=x^2u=x2 and v=exv=\mathrm{e}^{x}v=ex.
questions.why: The product rule (uv)′=u′v+uv′(uv)'=u'v+uv'(uv)′=u′v+uv′ has two terms. With u=x2u=x^2u=x2 and v=exv=\mathrm{e}^{x}v=ex the derivative is 2xex+x2ex=xex(2+x)2x\mathrm{e}^{x}+x^2\mathrm{e}^{x}=x\mathrm{e}^{x}(2+x)2xex+x2ex=xex(2+x); the student wrote only u′vu'vu′v, in effect treating ex\mathrm{e}^{x}ex as a constant. Differentiation does not distribute over a product at all — taking u=v=xu=v=xu=v=x, the false rule u′v′u'v'u′v′ would give 111 instead of the correct 2x2x2x. And ex\mathrm{e}^{x}ex really is its own derivative, so that part was sound.

questions.stem: When differentiating (2x−1)4(2x-1)^4(2x−1)4, which factor is most often dropped?
options: The power 444 standing in front.
A factor of ln⁡2\ln 2ln2.
None — the derivative is simply 4(2x−1)34(2x-1)^34(2x−1)3.
The factor 222, coming from the derivative of the inner function 2x−12x-12x−1.
questions.hint: Differentiate the outside first, leaving the bracket alone; then ask what the chain rule tells you to multiply by.
questions.why: The chain rule differentiates the outer function first, leaving the inside untouched, and then multiplies by the derivative of that inside. Here the inner derivative is 222, so the answer is 4(2x−1)3⋅2=8(2x−1)34(2x-1)^3\cdot2=8(2x-1)^34(2x−1)3⋅2=8(2x−1)3. The first option is precisely the error: it is what you get by treating the bracket as though it were a bare xxx. A logarithm appears when differentiating a constant raised to a variable power, such as 2x2^{x}2x, which is a different situation entirely.

questions.stem: What is lim⁡x→∞x3x2+1\displaystyle\lim_{x\to\infty}\frac{x^3}{x^2+1}x→∞lim​x2+1x3​?
options: 111, since both leading coefficients are 111.
000, since the denominator has more terms.
There is no finite limit — the quotient grows without bound.
13\tfrac1331​.
questions.hint: Compare the degrees, or divide top and bottom by x2x^2x2 and watch what each part does as x→∞x\to\inftyx→∞.
questions.why: Divide through by the highest power in the denominator: the expression becomes x1+1/x2\dfrac{x}{1+1/x^2}1+1/x2x​, whose numerator runs off to infinity while the denominator settles to 111. Comparing degrees is the quick route — a numerator of degree 333 beats a denominator of degree 222, so the quotient diverges. The ratio of leading coefficients is the answer only when the degrees are equal, and the limit is 000 only when the numerator has the smaller degree.

questions.stem: For a curve given parametrically, is d2ydx2=y¨x¨\dfrac{\mathrm{d}^2y}{\mathrm{d}x^2}=\dfrac{\ddot y}{\ddot x}dx2d2y​=x¨y¨​​?
options: No: differentiate dy/dx\mathrm{d}y/\mathrm{d}xdy/dx with respect to ttt, then divide by x˙\dot xx˙ again.
Yes, by the same reasoning that gives dy/dx=y˙/x˙\mathrm{d}y/\mathrm{d}x=\dot y/\dot xdy/dx=y˙​/x˙.
No — a second derivative cannot be obtained parametrically at all.
Yes, provided x¨≠0\ddot x\neq0x¨=0.
questions.hint: The first derivative is a ratio because of the chain rule. Apply that same chain rule again to dy/dx\mathrm{d}y/\mathrm{d}xdy/dx and see what you end up dividing by.
questions.why: The first derivative behaves like a ratio because the chain rule gives dydx=dy/dtdx/dt\dfrac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x}=\dfrac{\mathrm{d}y/\mathrm{d}t}{\mathrm{d}x/\mathrm{d}t}dxdy​=dx/dtdy/dt​. But the second derivative means differentiating dy/dx\mathrm{d}y/\mathrm{d}xdy/dx with respect to xxx, so the same chain rule applies once more: take d/dt\mathrm{d}/\mathrm{d}td/dt of dy/dx\mathrm{d}y/\mathrm{d}xdy/dx and divide by x˙\dot xx˙, not by x¨\ddot xx¨. For x=2tx=2tx=2t, y=t2−1y=t^2-1y=t2−1 the correct value is 12\tfrac1221​, whereas y¨/x¨\ddot y/\ddot xy¨​/x¨ would be 2/02/02/0. The parametric method works perfectly well — it is simply not the naive ratio.

questions.stem: In f′(x)=lim⁡h→0f(x+h)−f(x)hf'(x)=\lim_{h\to0}\dfrac{f(x+h)-f(x)}{h}f′(x)=limh→0​hf(x+h)−f(x)​, why can the limit not be evaluated by simply putting h=0h=0h=0?
options: Because the quotient is 00\tfrac{0}{0}00​ at h=0h=0h=0; the hhh has to be cancelled first.
Because the limit is only an approximation to the true derivative.
Because hhh is required to stay positive.
Because f(x+0)f(x+0)f(x+0) is undefined.
questions.hint: Put h=0h=0h=0 into the numerator and the denominator separately, before any cancelling, and see what each becomes.
questions.why: At h=0h=0h=0 the numerator is f(x)−f(x)=0f(x)-f(x)=0f(x)−f(x)=0 and the denominator is 000, so the quotient is the meaningless 00\tfrac0000​ — which is why the limit is taken as hhh approaches 000 rather than reaching it. The work is to simplify until the hhh in the denominator cancels: for f(x)=x2f(x)=x^{2}f(x)=x2, (x+h)2−x2h=2xh+h2h=2x+h\dfrac{(x+h)^{2}-x^{2}}{h}=\dfrac{2xh+h^{2}}{h}=2x+hh(x+h)2−x2​=h2xh+h2​=2x+h, and now h→0h\to0h→0 gives 2x2x2x safely. hhh approaches 000 from both sides, so it need not stay positive — insisting on one side gives a one-sided derivative, and that distinction is exactly what fails for ∣x∣\left|x\right|∣x∣ at 000. f(x+0)f(x+0)f(x+0) is simply f(x)f(x)f(x). And the limit is not an approximation: it is the definition.

questions.stem: Differentiating x2+y2=25x^{2}+y^{2}=25x2+y2=25 with respect to xxx, what is ddx(y2)\dfrac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}x}\left(y^{2}\right)dxd​(y2)?
options: 2y+dydx2y+\dfrac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x}2y+dxdy​
2ydydx2y\dfrac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x}2ydxdy​
000, since yyy is not xxx.
2y2y2y
questions.hint: Here yyy stands for a function of xxx, so y2y^{2}y2 is a function of a function. Which rule covers that, and what does it leave behind?
questions.why: yyy is a function of xxx, so y2y^{2}y2 is a composite and the chain rule applies: differentiate the outer square to get 2y2y2y, then multiply by the derivative of the inside, dydx\dfrac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x}dxdy​. That trailing factor is the whole of what makes implicit differentiation different from the ordinary kind, and dropping it is the single commonest slip on this topic. Treating yyy as a constant would give 000 and throw the equation away. Finishing the calculation: 2x+2ydydx=02x+2y\dfrac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x}=02x+2ydxdy​=0, so dydx=−xy\dfrac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x}=-\dfrac{x}{y}dxdy​=−yx​ — a derivative that depends on both coordinates, as it must on a circle.

questions.stem: Why does neither the power rule nor the exponential rule apply directly to y=xxy=x^{x}y=xx for x>0x>0x>0?
options: Because xxx^{x}xx is not differentiable.
Because the two rules give different answers and there is no way to choose between them.
Because xxx^{x}xx is undefined for x>0x>0x>0.
Because the power rule needs a constant exponent and the exponential rule a constant base, and here both vary.
questions.hint: Write down what each rule assumes about the base and about the exponent, then hold xxx^{x}xx against both lists.
questions.why: The power rule ddxxn=nxn−1\dfrac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}x}x^{n}=nx^{n-1}dxd​xn=nxn−1 assumes the exponent is constant; the exponential rule ddxax=axln⁡a\dfrac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}x}a^{x}=a^{x}\ln adxd​ax=axlna assumes the base is. In xxx^{x}xx both move, so neither rule is entitled to speak and the question of choosing between them does not arise. The way through is to take logarithms first: ln⁡y=xln⁡x\ln y=x\ln xlny=xlnx, and differentiating implicitly gives 1ydydx=ln⁡x+1\dfrac{1}{y}\dfrac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x}=\ln x+1y1​dxdy​=lnx+1, so dydx=xx(ln⁡x+1)\dfrac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x}=x^{x}\left(\ln x+1\right)dxdy​=xx(lnx+1). The same manoeuvre turns a long product or quotient into a sum before any differentiating is done. For x>0x>0x>0 the function is perfectly well defined and perfectly differentiable.
